segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the Sabbath was over, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices so that they could go and anoint him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And very early on the first day of the week they came to the tomb, when the sun had risen.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They were saying to one another,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And looking up, they saw that the stone had been rolled away, for it was extremely large.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Entering the tomb, they saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a white robe, and they were alarmed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he said to them,

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: “Do not be alarmed. You are looking for Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified. He has been raised; he is not here. Look, the place where they laid him.

segments.speaker: angel
segments.text: But go, tell his disciples and Peter, ‘He is going ahead of you into Galilee. There you will see him, just as he told you.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they went out and fled from the tomb, for trembling and bewilderment had seized them; and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid. ⟦But everything they had been instructed they reported briefly to Peter and those with him. And after this Jesus himself sent out through them, from east to west, the sacred and imperishable proclamation of eternal salvation. Amen.⟧

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: ⟦Now having risen early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had driven out seven demons.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She went and told those who had been with him, who were mourning and weeping.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And when they heard that he was alive and had been seen by her, they did not believe it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After this he showed himself in a different form to two of them as they were walking, on their way into the country.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They too went back and told the rest, but they did not believe them either.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Later he showed himself to the eleven themselves as they were reclining at table, and he reproached them for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who had seen him after he had been raised.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go into all the world and proclaim the good news to the whole creation.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And these signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will drive out demons; they will speak in new languages;

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: they will pick up snakes, and if they drink anything deadly it will certainly not harm them; they will lay hands on the sick, and they will get well.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then the Lord Jesus, after speaking to them, was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they went out and proclaimed everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the message through the signs that followed.⟧

notes.phrase: the first day of the week
notes.traditional: the first day of the week
notes.note: The Greek is literally 'the one of the sabbaths'. In Jewish Greek the word for Sabbath, especially in the plural, also meant the seven-day week, so the phrase means the day after the Sabbath, that is, Sunday.

Mark calls the figure simply a young man. The white robe and the message he delivers mark him as a heavenly messenger, and Matthew's parallel account speaks of an angel. Most interpreters read Mark the same way, though Mark himself does not use the word.

The Greek verb is passive in form. It can be read as a true passive, 'he has been raised' (that is, by God), or as an intransitive, 'he has risen'. Both are grammatically possible; the passive is chosen here because the New Testament regularly speaks of God raising Jesus, but the traditional rendering is not wrong.
This points back to Jesus' words on the way to the Mount of Olives (Mark 14:28), where he told the disciples that after being raised he would go ahead of them into Galilee.

The two earliest complete manuscripts of Mark, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (fourth century), end the Gospel with these words, and most scholars hold this to be the earliest ending that can be recovered. Whether Mark meant to stop this abruptly or an original ending was lost is disputed.

notes.phrase: But everything they had been instructed
notes.note: The double brackets mark the so-called shorter ending, which the Greek edition translated here prints as a later addition rather than part of Mark's own text. It is found in only a small number of manuscripts, almost always followed by the longer ending (verses 9–20), and its vocabulary is unlike Mark's.

notes.phrase: Now having risen early on the first day of the week
notes.note: The double brackets around verses 9–20 mark the longer ending. It appears in the great majority of manuscripts and was known by the late second century, but it is absent from the two earliest, joins awkwardly to verse 8, and differs from Mark in style and vocabulary. Nearly all scholars regard it as an early addition that draws on the resurrection accounts in the other Gospels and Acts; many churches nonetheless receive it as Scripture.

The Greek word was an ordinary one for good news, especially a public announcement of a victory or a ruler's accession. 'Gospel' is the traditional rendering and originally meant the same thing, but for many modern readers it has become a purely religious term or the name of a kind of book.

The Greek noun can mean creation as a whole or an individual created being, so the phrase can also be read 'to every creature', as in older English versions. In either case the sense is all humanity without restriction.

The Greek word is the ordinary one for the tongue and, by extension, a language. 'Tongues' is the traditional rendering and once meant simply 'languages', but in modern English it suggests a special religious phenomenon rather than what a Greek reader would have heard. How the speech described here relates to that in Acts 2 and 1 Corinthians 12–14 is debated.

notes.phrase: sat down at the right hand of God
notes.note: The wording echoes Psalm 110:1 ('Sit at my right hand'), the passage early Christians most often used to describe Jesus' exaltation. The seat at a king's right hand was the place of highest honour and shared authority.

Frequent across the New Testament and rendered either 'preach' or 'proclaim'; the cognate noun κήρυγμα (v. 8) should match.
The choice between 'tongues' and 'languages' must be made consistently for Mark 16, Acts 2, 10, 19 and 1 Corinthians 12–14.
Ranges over 'save', 'heal', 'rescue' and 'make well' across the New Testament, and needs a rule for when the theological and physical senses are distinguished.
Where it means the Christian proclamation, translators vary between 'the word' and 'the message', and it recurs constantly in Mark, Acts and the letters.
